Title: Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) bypass in matchRemotePattern
Analysis:
In Next.js, the `matchRemotePattern` function in `packages/next/src/shared/lib/match-remote-pattern.ts` validates whether an image source URL (`url`) matches the user-configured remote patterns (`remotePatterns`) in `next.config.js`.

The implementation of `matchRemotePattern` is as follows:
```typescript
  if (pattern.hostname === undefined) {
    throw new Error(
      `Pattern should define hostname but found\n${JSON.stringify(pattern)}`
    )
  } else {
    if (!makeRe(pattern.hostname).test(url.hostname)) {
      return false
    }
  }
```

Here, `makeRe(pattern.hostname)` is used to compile a glob pattern (e.g. `'*.example.com'`) into a JavaScript `RegExp`. However, `makeRe` compiles the glob pattern to match *anywhere* in the string if it does not have anchors, or it parses it as a regex. In `picomatch`, unless the glob matches the entire string, there can be vulnerabilities when matching hostnames if the glob doesn't compile to an strict regex.
Specifically, in `picomatch`, `makeRe` converts glob strings into regular expressions. But wait, how does `makeRe` behave under the hood?
Let's look at `makeRe` behaviour in `picomatch`. If `pattern.hostname` contains a glob pattern, or even if it's a literal hostname without globs, how does `picomatch` compile it?
If `pattern.hostname` is `example.com`, then `picomatch.makeRe('example.com')` compiles to a regex. Because of the dot (`.`) in `example.com`, picomatch compiles the dot as a literal dot `example\\.com` or as a glob character? In standard globbing, a dot `.` is a literal dot. However, does it anchor the regex?
Yes, `picomatch.makeRe` compiled regex usually includes `^` and `$` (i.e. `^(?:example\.com)$`), so a literal `example.com` will only match `example.com` exactly.
But what if the pattern contains wildcard character?
For example, if the hostname in remotePatterns is configured as `*.example.com` or `**.example.com`, `makeRe` translates this to a regex.

For `*.example.com`, `makeRe` translates it to a regex matching any subdomain of `example.com`. But what if a malicious actor requests a URL like `http://attacker.com/example.com` or something? No, `url.hostname` is the hostname of the requested image.

If `pattern.hostname` is `example.com`, `makeRe("example.com")` returns `/^(?:example\.com)$/`.
What if `pattern.hostname` is a glob like `*.example.com`?
`makeRe("*.example.com")` compiles to a regex: `/^(?:(?!\.)(?=.)[^/]*?\.example\.com)$/` or similar.
But wait! What if the user inputs a hostname with special regex characters or glob characters in a way that allows bypassing the match? Or what if a URL is structured to bypass `url.hostname` parsing?
Let's consider how `new URL(url)` parses hostnames.
In Node.js:
`new URL('https://example.com\\attacker.com')`
Wait! In the WHATWG URL spec, backslashes `\` are normalized to forward slashes `/` in the authority/host parser if the protocol is a special protocol (like `https:`).
Wait, if `url` is `https://example.com\\attacker.com`, the WHATWG `new URL` parser converts the backslash into a forward slash, making the URL `https://example.com/attacker.com`, so `url.hostname` becomes `example.com` and `url.pathname` becomes `/attacker.com`.
